topline: Three stories today: Bulgaria elects Moscow-dialogue advocate Iliana Iotova as president in a low-turnout runoff, the European Commission backs the Polish parliament's right to fill the Constitutional Tribunal, and a new €2 EU handling fee on non-EU e-commerce parcels takes effect.

stories.title: Bulgaria's acting president Iotova wins runoff on a platform of dialogue with Moscow
stories.summary: Acting President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria, won Sunday's presidential runoff against Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister supported by the pro-Western opposition. Exit polls and parallel counts put her between roughly 51% and 58%, against about 39% to 45% for Gyurov, with turnout of around 27–29% after a record-low 23% in the first round; official results were expected on Monday. Iotova, who stepped up when Radev resigned the presidency in January to run for parliament, favours negotiations with Russia and opposes military aid to Ukraine while backing EU and NATO membership; she said she wants Bulgaria 'strong in a strong Europe'. Gyurov accepted the result and called for unity. The vote was overshadowed by October drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, which left 21 people missing; Commission President von der Leyen congratulated Iotova.
stories.why: Bulgaria's presidency is largely ceremonial but holds treaty-signing and veto powers and commands the armed forces, so a second Moscow-friendly voice alongside Radev could complicate EU unanimity on sanctions and Ukraine support from a frontline Black Sea state.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage leads with Iotova's position on Russia and Ukraine, setting it against Black Sea security fears and an electorate that largely stayed home. It gives space to critics who say she has not clearly blamed Moscow for the drone attacks, and to voters casting a 'lesser evil' ballot; taz's pre-runoff reporting framed her bluntly as the Kremlin-friendly favourite.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Stresses the drone attacks, record-low turnout and an analyst's view that her response to Russian threats was unconvincing.

outlets.name: taz
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (pre-runoff): casts the race as a pro-Western challenger fighting an uphill battle.

right.angle: No dedicated right-leaning take on the runoff result was found in the outlets checked by publication time. Right-leaning European outlets had not yet framed Iotova's win around sovereignty, sanctions or Ukraine policy.

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets treat the result mainly as a Russia-security story and a sign of disengagement; a comparable right-leaning framing was not yet available.

stories.title: Commission says Polish parliament has the right to seat new Constitutional Tribunal judges
stories.summary: A European Commission spokesperson said on Saturday that appointing eight new members of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal lies within the constitutional power of the Sejm, and that Polish authorities must keep the court functioning in line with EU case law. The Commission also pointed to a May 2026 European Court of Human Rights interim measure telling Poland not to obstruct the judges the Sejm elected in March. The statement follows Friday night's confrontation at the tribunal, where President Karol Nawrocki, who has refused to swear in the new judges, entered the building after the court's PiS-era chief was suspended. In a televised address, Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the scenes scandalous and said there could be no concessions on restoring independent courts, while PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński accused the government of building a police state. The tribunal's acting head has called the judges to meet on Tuesday.
stories.why: Brussels is now openly siding with one camp in a constitutional dispute between a member state's government and its president, a test of how the EU applies rule-of-law standards after years of conflict with the previous PiS government.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage presents the suspension of the tribunal's leadership as a step toward undoing PiS's grip on the court, citing EU and ECHR rulings that the tribunal is not independent. It casts Nawrocki and PiS as defending a political bastion, and describes the crowds outside the court as largely right-wing.

outlets.name: taz
outlets.note: Frames the clash as Poland's right fighting to keep a power instrument; notes most constitutional lawyers back the Sejm's judges.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage adopts the language of an attempted 'judicial coup', leading with Nawrocki turning his plane around to defend the court and with reports of pressure on his staff. It stresses claims of politically motivated prosecutions and treats the government's legal case as the contested side; ECR leaders urged EU institutions not to look away.

outlets.name: Hungarian Conservative
outlets.note: Portrays Nawrocki's night-time entry as stopping an unlawful takeover by pro-Tusk judges.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (14 October): describes the government's moves as a forcible takeover of the court.

stories.differ: The left sees Brussels endorsing a repair of judicial independence; the right sees a government seizing a constitutional body with the Commission's blessing.

stories.title: EU's €2 handling fee on non-EU online parcels takes effect
stories.summary: From 1 November the EU charges a €2 handling fee on e-commerce goods arriving from outside the bloc, on top of the temporary €3 duty on low-value items introduced in July. The fee is paid by platforms, sellers or carriers and is meant to cover the cost of customs checks; reports differ on whether it is levied per parcel or per item type. About 5 million small parcels still enter the EU daily, 91% of them from China in 2024, although the Commission says small-parcel imports fell 60% between July and September. A Commission document reported by Reuters estimates the charges could raise about €6 billion a year for the EU budget in 2028–2034. AliExpress warned the costs would hit low-income households, while the European Parliament's lead lawmaker on customs reform defended targeting non-compliant imports from platforms such as Temu and Shein.
stories.why: The fee is a test of the EU's customs overhaul and its push to curb cheap Chinese imports, and it is being eyed as a new 'own resource' for the next long-term EU budget.

left.angle: Centre-left coverage found was earlier and largely factual, presenting the fee as a customs-cost measure aimed at the flood of low-value parcels from outside the bloc. No distinct left-leaning commentary on its entry into force was found by publication time.

outlets.name: Le Monde
outlets.note: Earlier coverage (26 October): straight report on the fee and its rationale.

right.angle: Right-leaning French coverage presents the fee as Europe tightening control over Shein and Temu parcels, putting enforcement first. A fuller right-leaning argument, for example on costs to consumers, was not found by publication time.

outlets.name: Le JDD
outlets.note: Headline frames the fee as a tool to better control parcels from the Chinese platforms.

stories.differ: Partisan framing is muted: both sides mostly report the fee as a control measure, with the sharpest criticism coming from the platforms and Chinese commentators rather than from either political camp.
